intent: Motivating case. Show how agent-inferred execution details can depart from user intent, and how targeted clarification keeps actions within user-confirmed intent.
paper: Research topic: Agent intent safety during tool execution. This is a proposed method, with no measured results. The central risk is converting the agent's own interpretation into execution authority. Motivating fictional case: a user says, "Share three final reports with Li Ming. Organize old versions. Create a local checklist." The final report files are already identified. A permitted contact lookup finds two different people named Li Ming. Neither conversation nor existing policy fixes the sharing access level. Organizing old files could mean archive or delete. Show a rich readable case-study diagram with a user instruction, three document icons, two contact candidates, and uncertain fields Recipient=?, Access=?, Old-file action=?. Show an unsafe branch in restrained coral: the agent guesses a recipient, edit access, and deletion, yielding misdelivery or unwanted deletion. An external document recommending a personal mailbox is an untrusted suggestion whose provenance stays separate from user authorization. Show the proposed safe branch in teal: identify the uncertain intent elements, ask "Which Li Ming and which access?", receive "Partner Li Ming; read-only for these three reports", update only recipient/access for those reports, and share the three reports. The independent local checklist can be completed immediately. Old-file action stays unresolved and its operation waits for clarification. Use blue for user-expressed intent, amber for uncertainty, coral for deviation, teal for confirmed execution. Do not imply that a generic safety filter resolves ambiguity or that all tools require confirmation. Preserve a visible chain from user intent to actual tool effects. No quantitative performance chart. Short English labels, title exactly "Agent Intent Safety: A Project Handoff".

intent: Problem abstraction. Reveal how incomplete intent is concretized into tool parameters and how unsupported assumptions acquire real effects.
paper: Research topic: Agent intent safety, not generic harmful-content detection. Create the problem-definition figure for a proposed runtime method. The main visual backbone is User-expressed intent -> Agent plan -> Tool arguments -> Real-world effects. The user expresses goals and constraints, while the agent must choose an action, object, recipient, scope and conditions. Show three explicit unresolved elements beneath this backbone: ambiguous recipient identity, uncertain archive/delete action, unspecified sharing scope/access. At the transition from plan to tool arguments, show inferred parameters being filled in and turning into wrong-recipient sharing or deletion. A separate external-context lane supplies a document suggestion; retain a provenance tag "External content" and show where treating it as authority could shift execution intent. A user-evidence lane carries confirmed constraints toward the execution boundary. Distinguish Known facts, User-confirmed intent, and Unresolved authorization in three small legible state examples. Use the running example of three final reports and old drafts. A tool-capable account can execute share/delete; task-specific intent still needs to support the selected effect. Highlight the research question: "Which effects are grounded in user intent?" and a secondary question "What should we clarify next?" The intervention is located before tool submission. Keep the user-intent backbone visible in every panel. The figure describes risk and method scope, with no experimental accuracy or success rates. Use the same restrained blue/amber/coral/teal scheme as other figures in this set, white background, short English labels. Title exactly "Where Intent Deviates Before Tool Execution".

intent: Abstract method. Show a closed runtime loop that grounds permitted effects in user intent and selects clarifications under limited interaction budget.
paper: Proposed method for agent intent safety: maintain the distinction between user-expressed goals, user-confirmed execution constraints, agent hypotheses, and external content throughout execution. Draw a conceptual system with User request and dialogue -> Evidence-backed authorization state -> Authorization-condition / task-obligation dependency graph -> Budget-aware clarification choice -> User answer -> Scoped state update -> Execution check -> Authorized tool effects. The loop returns updated state and remaining obligations to the next decision. Each authorization field carries explicit or unresolved status, object/scope and source evidence. The graph has field nodes Recipient R, Access P, Old-file action C and obligations Share technical note T1, Share test report T2, Share deployment guide T3, Organize old versions T4. R and P jointly enable each of T1,T2,T3. C enables T4. Draw actual AND dependencies so either R or P alone cannot enable sharing. An already authorized local-checklist task proceeds on its own lane. Budget is the remaining user confirmation effort. In an explicitly labeled illustrative valid-answer branch, budget 1 chooses C and completes one obligation; budget 2 can choose R then P and complete three sharing obligations. These counts are a toy-case walkthrough, not experimental results and not a universal guarantee over refusal answers. A denied or unresolved answer leaves the affected route unavailable and triggers re-evaluation. The primary objective is to preserve user-confirmed intent at the execution boundary while advancing the requested task. Show confirmed fields turning teal and unresolved ones staying amber after a scoped user answer. Every arrow should connect a real part of this loop. All visual labels short English, title exactly "Preserving User Intent Through Clarification".

intent: Concrete algorithm. Connect authorization-semantic LoRA training, GraphSAGE multi-step clarification value learning, and the runtime intent-preserving execution loop.
paper: Proposed implementation of agent intent safety. Draw an integrated method figure with clearly separated offline training and online runtime, connected by learned models. Module A: Qwen3-8B with LoRA learns authorization semantics using supervised examples of ambiguous actions/objects/scopes, source confusion, and multi-turn updates. Supervision is field status + operation/object/scope + original-text evidence. Mini training pair: "Organize old drafts" gives Action=unresolved; user answer "Archive; do not delete" gives Action=archive and Constraint=no deletion. Initial request parsing and reply parsing share the same learned parser. Online parser consumes user dialogue and labeled external context, produces evidence-backed authorization fields; it does not invent authority from external content. Fixed tool-effect contracts map candidate tool calls to required authorization conditions. Build a bipartite graph of authorization fields and user task obligations, including shared conditions and AND requirements. Module B: two GraphSAGE layers encode this graph; candidate-question embedding + pooled graph state + remaining confirmation budget feed an MLP estimating safe task completion reachable after this question. Offline multi-step planning creates value labels using the minimum over explicitly modeled answer branches. Multi-step behavior is learned from these planning labels. No claim that two graph layers alone perform multi-step planning. Show next-question selection -> actual user answer -> shared LoRA parser -> source/scope/question/version checks -> local authorization update -> execution check -> authorized effects, and feedback to graph. Annotate the budget example R AND P -> three sharing tasks, C -> old-file organization, using compact graph nodes. Emphasize that all components serve preservation of user-expressed and confirmed intent through tool execution. This is a proposed system, without fabricated benchmark scores, trained-model results or absolute safety guarantees. Use a consistent blue user-input lane, violet learned models, amber uncertain state, and teal confirmed effects. Title exactly "Learning to Ground and Clarify Agent Intent".
